examples: 에 attaches to the time word
nuance: 정오 is the formal word for 12:00 in the daytime, a bit more written or precise than just 낮 (daytime). In everyday speech people often say 낮 12시 instead, but 정오 is clear and common in schedules and announcements.
mistakes: Confusing 정오 (noon, 12 p.m.) with 자정 (midnight, 12 a.m.).
Saying 정오 시 — just use 정오 by itself, not with 시.

nuance: 자정 means 12:00 at night, the moment the day changes. It pairs with 정오 (noon) as its daytime opposite. In casual talk people may say 밤 12시, but 자정 is the standard single-word term.
mistakes: Mixing up 자정 (midnight) and 정오 (noon).
Using 자정 for late evening in general — it specifically means 12 a.m.

english: dawn, the small hours (early morning before sunrise)
usage: at dawn / in the small hours
use native-ish 시 reading for the hour
nuance: 새벽 covers the dark, early hours roughly from 1 a.m. to sunrise, before 아침 (morning) begins. Koreans attach it to clock times to show they mean a.m.: 새벽 4시 is 4 in the morning. It carries a feeling of very early or staying up late.
mistakes: Confusing 새벽 (pre-dawn hours) with 아침 (morning after sunrise).
Forgetting that 새벽 signals a.m., so 새벽 3시 ≠ 3 in the afternoon.

english: midday, the middle of the day (broad daylight)
usage: the brightest, hottest part of the day
in the middle of the day
examples: It's too hot in the middle of the day.
I took a walk at midday.
nuance: 한낮 means the very middle of the daytime, around noon when the sun is highest and strongest. It is more vivid than plain 낮 and often appears when talking about heat or bright sun. Its night-time counterpart is 한밤중 (the dead of night).
mistakes: Using 한낮 for any daytime — it specifically means around noon.
Mixing up 한낮 (midday) with 한밤중 (middle of the night).

english: the middle of the night, the dead of night
usage: in the middle of the night
even in the dead of night
until the middle of the night
examples: A call came in the middle of the night.
I woke up in the middle of the night.
I worked until the middle of the night.
nuance: 한밤중 is the deepest part of the night, around midnight, when everything is dark and quiet. It is more vivid than just 밤 (night) and often suggests an unusual or inconvenient hour. Its daytime counterpart is 한낮 (midday).
mistakes: Using 한밤중 for early evening — it means deep night, near midnight.
Mixing up 한밤중 (middle of the night) with 한낮 (midday).

usage: 에 is often dropped: 올해 + verb
examples: I came to Korea this year.
에 can be dropped after 올해
I'm twenty years old this year.
nuance: 올해 means the present year and is used directly before a verb, usually without 에: 올해 졸업해요 (I graduate this year). It sits between 작년 (last year) and 내년 (next year). Use 금년 only in very formal writing.
mistakes: Adding 에 unnaturally — 올해 갔어요 is more natural than 올해에 갔어요.
Confusing 올해 (this year) with 오늘 (today).

examples: I came to Korea last year.
I've been learning Korean since last year.
nuance: 작년 means the year before the current one and very often takes 에 when used as a time point: 작년에 만났어요 (we met last year). It is the everyday word; 지난해 is a slightly more formal synonym. It pairs with 올해 and 내년.
mistakes: Forgetting 에 in time-point sentences: prefer 작년에 갔어요.
Mixing up 작년 (last year) with 어제 (yesterday).

examples: I'm going to Korea next year.
nuance: 내년 means the year after the present one and usually takes 에 as a time point: 내년에 시작해요 (it starts next year). It completes the set with 작년 (last year) and 올해 (this year). 다음 해 is a more literal phrasing but 내년 is the common word.
mistakes: Confusing 내년 (next year) with 내일 (tomorrow).
Dropping 에 where it is natural: prefer 내년에 가요.

usage: set phrase: 종일 = the whole day
examples: I eat three times a day.
I want to rest just one day.
nuance: 하루 is the noun for a single day and appears in many set phrases, especially 하루 종일 (all day long) and 하루에 ... 번 (... times a day). For counting more days you switch to 이틀, 사흘, and so on. It can also mean 'one day' in the sense of a particular day.
mistakes: Saying 하루 번 — use 하루에 한 번 for 'once a day'.
Using 하루 to mean 'today'; 'today' is 오늘.

english: a few days; what date / which day
examples: We met a few days ago.
I was sick for a few days.
nuance: 며칠 has two everyday uses: 'a few days' (며칠 동안 쉬었어요) and 'what date' (며칠이에요?). It is spelled 며칠, never 몇일. Tone and context tell you whether someone is estimating a number of days or asking the date.
mistakes: Spelling it 몇일 — the correct form is always 며칠.
Confusing 며칠 (what date) with 무슨 요일 (what day of the week).

usage: a point in the past or future
examples: Back then I was a student.
used for a future agreed time
nuance: 그때 points to a specific moment already known to both speakers, in the past ('back then') or a planned future ('see you then'). It is written as one word, 그때. Compare 이때 (this time, now) and 언제 (when, the question word).
mistakes: Writing it as two words 그 때 — the standard form is 그때.
Using 그때 for a brand-new time the listener doesn't know yet.

nuance: 나중 means a later, unspecified time and is almost always used as 나중에 ('later, afterward'). It is perfect for postponing things politely: 나중에 이야기해요 (let's talk later). Compare 이따가 (in a little while, same day) and 다음에 (next time).
mistakes: Using 나중 without 에 — the natural form is 나중에.
Confusing 나중에 (later, vague) with 다음에 (next time).
